method: Ordered finite two-school review of every available subsection in Tzidkat HaTzadik 60–264. Each entry records its actual comparisons, including rejections; completion of the full range is reported only when all available references have an entry. The missing Siman 74 is an unavailable source, never a completed conceptual review.

entries.assessment: Read the whole argument from pain and rebuke through Jehu, the inn, and the sotah waters. Retain the existing parapet comparison: the recipient's liability never releases the person administering rebuke from responsibility. The additional candidates do not improve that precise relation.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Rejected: concealment and suffering generate Oral Torah, whereas this siman tests the culpability of the human instrument causing another's suffering.
Retained: the whole discourse explains why another person's possible fall requires a parapet in one's own service, including the limiting cases of shame, Abaye, and Shlomo.
Rejected: Yehudah's concealed worth and the correction of his judgment do not explain the rebuker's duty to be personally clear of the fault.

entries.assessment: Read the entire progression from priestly holiness to added commandments, practical alacrity, inward separation, and the enduring covenant even when holiness is concealed. Retain Yisrael Kedoshim's distinction between the enduring common body and differing visible expressions. Do not turn a shared Korach verse into an additional parallel.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained: its whole paragraph distinguishes inherited belonging from the actual work of sanctification, then places Aharon within Israel's organic shared life.

Rejected for this anchor: its central mechanism is continuous divine sustenance and revelation through removing concealment, rather than the persistence of priestly holiness through inherited membership.

entries.assessment: Read all inherited spiritual names, the exception of the crown of Torah, and the concluding explanation of differing tribes and schools. Preserve the Dover qualification that a convert's acquired name is nevertheless a true name; the examined Noach passage concerns a different distinction between temporal and eternal covenantal continuance.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained: it expressly interprets the same verse about converts, distinguishing acquired naming from birth while affirming genuine belonging and a tribal inheritance.

Rejected after reading paragraphs 1–6: Noach's limited prayer for descendants explains temporal survival versus eternal continuance, not the distribution of spiritual names or Torah's nonhereditary crown.

entries.assessment: Read the distinctions between maternal and paternal resemblance, birth and habitual education, and the final received teaching about the hidden parental heart. Approve Kometz's separate account of learned, ancestral, and inborn dispositions, retaining its conclusion that none determines the direction of divine service by itself. The Ishbitz comparisons examined do not establish the source of the received teaching.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: its three names distinguish education, family, and birth, then qualify how each is redirected through divine guidance. This clarifies the siman's express distinction between habit and origin.

Rejected: the specific correction of Yoav's teacher concerns the dependence of a daughter's established qualities on her father's service; it does not explain the siman's precise maternal/paternal distinction or identify the received tradition.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Rejected: Yaakov's uncertainty before blessing his sons explains the development from rebuke to mercy, not the manifestation of a parent's concealed qualities in descendants.
Rejected: habitual avodah becoming joyful freedom is not an account of resemblance transmitted between parent and child.

entries.assessment: Read all four examples: apparent assistance, Eliyahu's concealment, the oven dispute, and the protest after Korach. Retain the existing distinction between reliance and following personal inclination. The further sources concern sustenance despite unworthiness or the need to remove self-interest; neither establishes that miraculous assistance is proof of correctness.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained: the complete paragraph explicitly rejects following the heart without effort on the strength of divine assistance and makes the promised protection conditional on sincere exertion.
Rejected: assistance to an impoverished petitioner distinguishes undeserved sustenance from Torah's plenitude; the shared Isaiah verse does not supply the epistemic distinction about signs.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 7
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not added: removing personal benefit is a concrete discipline for Avraham's uncertain action; its later discussion includes a distinct R. Akiva qualification and cannot be flattened into a universal rule about all signs.

entries.assessment: Read the opening surrender, the explanation of the incense offerers' error about the future, their real elevation despite culpability, and Moshe and Aharon's responsive falling on their faces. Retain Tiferet Yosef's intercession for the community, and add Beit Yaakov's separate explanation of surrender within the requested content of prayer. The source contains a numeral discrepancy, 248 in Hebrew versus 250 in English; record it for textual verification without silently rewriting the canonical manuscript.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined: the complete paragraph explains nefilat apayim as surrender following spoken prayer and the bounds of time, place, and soul. It is sound background, but no further note is added because the two retained comparisons already explain the needed distinctions without multiplying similar opening quotations.
Retained: its whole discussion turns Moshe and Aharon's surrender into intercession grounded in the soul's root above the reach of sin, including concern for every soul capable of repair.
Approved: the whole paragraph expounds the same Psalm as a condition within prayer, yielding the requested benefit if it would draw the petitioner away from divine service.

entries.assessment: Read the complete argument distinguishing the need for daily prayer even after a favorable decree from intensified prayer to tear a decree. Retain the Ishbitz account of Eliyahu's prayer for the generation. Takanat HaShavin's qualification of a sealed decree concerns the distinction between inward repentance and its outward realization and is not added as though it simply denied this siman.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. It distinguishes the heart's repentance from external penalties and the final repair. Its complex use of a decree not being torn would require explaining a different question, rather than clarifying the daily-prayer distinction here.

Retained after reading the whole discourse: Eliyahu's personal crisis is interpreted as a summons to pray for the generation's return, so the desired rain is realized through intercession rather than mere knowledge of divine purpose.

entries.assessment: Read the full siman: repentance accepted at one level can be renewed at a higher level, and the new distress can itself belong to the ascent. Approve Likkutei Maamarim's distinction between divine forgiveness and the person's continuing acknowledgment. Beit Yaakov offers a shorter complementary formulation but does not itself explain the successive levels, so no second similar quotation is added.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: the full paragraph distinguishes the divine act of abundant forgiveness from the person's permanent acknowledgment of deficiency, retaining the qualification that claiming no failure on one's own authority recreates the failure.
Rejected: the concealment of sins before the attribute of judgment in the account of Yaakov and Esav is a different question from renewed repentance at successive levels.

Examined with paragraphs 7, 9, and 10: it makes remembrance of sin and divine overlooking complementary. Not added because the longer Likkutei selection better preserves the distinction needed here and avoids an isolated dependent clause.

entries.assessment: Read the progression from bodily commandments to the heart, the quiet voice, and the necessary preliminary battle with the inclination. Retain Peri Tzadik's distinction between noisy preparation and settled attachment. Add the Ishbitz explanation of why commandments are called counsels: their aim reaches the bodily will as well as a momentary feeling of love or awe.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained: the whole discourse explicitly makes wind, noise, and fire preparations for quiet attachment, while preserving the distinct work of each stage.
Not selected as an additional quotation: this paragraph supplies the Zohar citation for David's emptied heart, but does not itself add an explanation of the preliminary struggle versus settled rule.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Tiferet Yosef, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 3
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: the complete discussion asks what the 613 counsels aim at, since love and awe are already individual commandments, and answers that they bring the embodied will into accord with Hashem.

entries.assessment: Read the full sequence of the nations receiving good qualities through Israel, Ahab's victory and forfeiture, and Mordechai's fear of Heaven. The sources examined explain other aspects of the same examples but do not adequately establish the precise judicial mechanism claimed here. No additional conceptual footnote is approved in this finite pass.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Rejected for this argument: the debate over writing Esther treats the nations' response as evidence of a manifest miracle, not the transfer of a good quality as the ground of Israel's right to victory.
Not approved: the paragraph states that a wicked person must contain some good to exist; this is not yet the siman's specific account of another nation's indebtedness to Israel's good influence.

Read in full but not approved: Israel's endurance in dispersion becomes the human awakening for the future Jerusalem; that is a different causal relation from Ahab losing his victory through calling the enemy his brother.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 5
candidatesReviewed.reason: Read in full but not approved: the wells distinguish shared knowledge and sacrifice from Israel's distinctive endurance. This does not explain the particular transmission-and-judgment mechanism of the siman.

entries.assessment: Read the entire relation of deficiency and repair, the fig leaves, the birth of Mashiach, resurrection, the red heifer, and the two messianic roots. Retain the existing Ishbitz comparison because it explains how ashes that appear lifeless can purify. The examined Machshavot Charutz paragraph gives sound background to the festival and David's enduring life but adds less to the exact repair-through-the-same-substance argument.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Read in full; not added. Its distinction between preparation in potential and actual disclosure, and its interpretation of David's requested life, is background rather than a new explanation of why the instrument of deficiency becomes the means of repair.

Retained after reading the whole paragraph: it explains the precedence of purification to corpse impurity and then distinguishes earth's growth from ashes, locating the enduring root of life beyond the observer's apparent loss.
Not selected as a stand-alone source: the paragraph only refers to an explanation in Chukat and supplies no complete explanatory thought to quote here.

entries.assessment: Read all limits on seeking another's downfall, including the distinction between harm to Heaven and harm to people, Elisha's punishment, David's unusual freedom from self-interest, and the prior psalm's favorable judgment. Add Tiferet Yosef's explicit explanation of the interpreters of the remnant: they enlarge the remaining good rather than treating a verdict as the exhaustion of a person's possibility.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full: David's uprooting of the inclination is treated as an exceptional divine aid, with a further qualification arising from his generation. This supports caution about generalizing his condition; no additional quotation is needed alongside the more precise ending comparison.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 20:1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined with paragraphs 2–3: it explains why Avraham's new moral demand provoked hostility, but not the conditions of permissible judgment or the requirement to precede it with goodwill.

Approved: its whole argument distinguishes the mixed present from final separation and expressly explains how the interpreters of the remnant seek the good point even in those assigned no share in the world to come.

entries.assessment: Read the distinctions between miracles through Torah and through prayer, the reason temporary events can be recorded for generations, and the final distinction between quantity of effect and enduring greatness. Retain the existing account of lasting gates, and add Peri Tzadik's explanation that a prophetic word may achieve its reception in later generations even if it was resisted at the time.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after reading the complete discourse: Jeremiah's words are ultimately heard although his immediate hearers resisted them; the author explicitly connects that later efficacy with the rule about prophecy needed for generations.

Retained after reading the whole discussion: preparation from below gives the prophetic attainment enduring availability, distinguishing a momentary visitation from what remains for later generations.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 33:2
candidatesReviewed.reason: The beginning was examined but not approved or counted as a completed target reading; the displayed text was truncated. It is not used as evidence for an additional note.

entries.assessment: Read the entire account of providentially occasioned proof of repentance, the prohibition on creating a forbidden test, the stages of Gehazi's repair, and the continuing need for Elisha's acceptance. Retain Takanat HaShavin's essential distinction between inward repentance and evidence restoring public trust. The examined Ishbitz discourse does not improve that specific distinction.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained after reading the whole paragraph: inward resolution can constitute real repentance at that moment while public reliance requires observed conduct; later failure must be assessed with the paragraph's express qualifications.

Read in full; not added. It distinguishes the present work of separating and gaining good from the final completed separation at resurrection, but does not address the sequence of an occasioned test and restored personal trust.

entries.assessment: Read the full analogy between redeemable monetary sanctity and intrinsic bodily sanctity, the exception concerning Esav's birthright, and the final contrast of transferable good and evil. Add Yisrael Kedoshim's exact account of the apparent versus inward birthright and Beit Yaakov's account of love rooted beyond changes in action. Do not mistake a shared substitution verse for an explanation of intrinsic sanctity.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not added: its examples of substitution in the birth and survival of children illustrate the verse but do not explain the distinction between essential and incidental possession made here.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 5
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not added: the replacement of Shlomo by Bilaam is followed by an account of wisdom and the birth of a soul within Israel; it would distract from the specific intrinsic-sanctity distinction.
Approved: the complete paragraph expressly distinguishes Esav's visible precedence at birth from Yaakov's inward priority, and explains why borrowed outward sanctity could pass away.
Read in full; not added. It treats the danger of apparent independent existence and the inward shelter of Sukkot, rather than the precise question of redeemable and intrinsic sanctity.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Read in full; not added. The complex contrast of Yosef and Yehudah and the chief baker's substitution supplies an example but not the most direct account of the nonredeemable spiritual bond.
Approved: the whole paragraph explicitly places the love for Avraham beyond the reach of actions and connects that enduring choice with the same Song of Songs verse.

entries.assessment: Read the entire argument about the opposite possibilities of a prepared moment, including the Flood and false confidence before the destruction. Retain the Cheshvan comparison, which explains the same prepared water as Torah or destruction and keeps the condition of repentance explicit. The further candidates do not warrant another general note about desire.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained after reading the whole teaching: the forty days can establish new Torah or become destructive waters depending on the response, and the account expressly explains why the Flood remains a present calendar reference.

Examined in full: the generation of the Flood and Moshe's Torah explain repair of the root of evil, but the existing Cheshvan source more directly develops the two contrary outcomes of the prepared time.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not added: desire giving birth to true Torah, and Torah renewing desire in age, do not themselves explain why the same prepared moment can become destruction.

entries.assessment: Read the opening genealogical caution together with the decisive exception of Torah's crown, broken vessels, Rabbi Akiva, and the Kenites. Retain the Ki Tavo source because it develops the concealed Oral Torah roots of the precise examples; do not detach the opening caution from that substantial exception.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained after full reading: the paragraph explains Rabbi Akiva, Sisera, the Kenites, and Otniel as recoveries of the Oral Torah's concealed root, directly developing this siman's examples.
Examined but not added: the selected Zohar paragraph distinguishes Yehoshua's lower receiving level for the war against Amalek; it does not develop Torah's crown being open regardless of ancestry.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
candidatesReviewed.reason: Read in full but not used here: kingship beginning with self-rule does not independently explain the contrast between lineage and the crown of Torah.

entries.assessment: Read the entire argument, including the qualification about Avraham's descendants, Chizkiyahu and Menashe, rejoicing at the announcement of children, and the apparently opposing Tanchuma. Retain Poked Akarim's distinction between petition and unsolicited divine promise. Add the independently illuminating account of Avraham rescuing Lot because an initially hidden royal line would emerge.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained after reading the full paragraph: a divine promise of children and a person's request have different epistemic positions; the paragraph expressly resolves the same Tanchuma and Menashe difficulty.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 38:1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not added: Ishmael's relation to Sarah and the maintenance of bodily powers concern a different evaluation of family branches.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved for this siman after full reading: Shem cannot initially understand saving Lot, and then discovers that the permitted female lines of Ammon and Moab yield the Davidic and Solomonic kingship.

entries.assessment: Read the full eclipse analogy, including the reflected moonlight, the degrees of exile, and the final distinction concerning the nations. Retain Chanukah's account of received light and add Kometz's express distinction between the light at its source and its absence for recipients. The additional Ishbitz account treats embodied reception more generally.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained after full reading: written and Oral Torah are compared with intrinsic and received light, preserving the claim that the human-seeming innovation is also a divine gift.
Approved: the whole short teaching expressly distinguishes the observer's eclipse from a loss in the sun itself and relates the differing analogies to the diminution of the heavenly retinue.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 11:1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. Straight, reversed, and restored reception explains prayer and the crossing of the sea, but is less precise for the siman's distinction between the source and its recipient.

entries.assessment: Read all three repairs: anger and place, desire and conduct, honor and name; retain the limits illustrated by Ahab's failed claim to Gilead. Add Peri Tzadik's explanation of Moshe's relation to anger and the refuge cities, alongside the existing Ishbitz account of refuge through clearer recognition of providence.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after full reading: it distinguishes Moshe's exceptional purity from anger, Pinchas's particular task, and Moshe's burial in the region whose refuge cities answer the prevalence of murder.
Retained after full reading: Moshe's clarity about providence provides the refuge-city protection and a possibility of repair even for the lowliest soul.

entries.assessment: Read the whole succession argument, Moshe's envy, the land-of-Israel qualification, and the dream interpretation that parents' and children's long lives can coexist through alternating disclosure. The reviewed comparisons clarify receiving and complementary service; add the concrete Mishkan comparison as an account of the inward attitude that makes room for another person's visible role.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sefer HaZikhronot, Mitzvot, Positive Commandment 3, Chapter 5 3
candidatesReviewed.reason: Rejected: the halakhic discussion of seeing a clear sky after cloud concerns the same image, not envy or succession.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 25
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full: Moshe and Yehoshua's receiving, uncertainty, and intellectual poverty explain a related succession problem; no extra quotation is needed alongside the clearer selected account of complementary roles.
Approved: the complete paragraph treats the honor of Heaven produced by ark and curtain makers as complementary, after explaining how exclusion of another member compromises the whole.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Tiferet Yosef, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 5
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. Its Jordan and anger symbolism explains the conditions for continued human work, rather than this siman's specific possibility of making room for a successor.

entries.assessment: Read the full distinction between bodily settlement and continued inward wandering, including Cain's partial reprieve and the love of one's place. The compared sources treat partial atonement and ordinary attachment to place, but neither adequately explains this precise movement from repaired action to repaired thought; no additional parallel is approved in this pass.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full: suffering and repentance complete distinct halves in the account of the Akeidah and Cain. It does not establish the siman's specific equation of settlement and the correction of thought.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 31:11
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not approved: it explains attachment to one's native place as fixedness in the account of Avraham's soul and body. The shared phrase about the charm of a place does not supply the distinct repentance mechanism here.

entries.assessment: Read both kinds of finding, the difference between Noach's finding grace and Israel being found, the qualification of the labor maxim, and the final examples of employing another to seek finds. Add the account of an insight exceeding the effort that prepared for it, preserving the distinction between preparation and control of the result.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after full reading: the paragraph expressly explains why attained wisdom is called a find, since one could not previously direct effort toward that still-unknown attainment.
Examined in full; not added. The blessings of reception, protection, and gratitude for a small portion do not specifically explain an unexpected find or its relation to effort.
Examined with paragraphs 1 and 3; not added. It supplies the same Midrash of undeserved grace, but the comparison read here does not improve on the siman's own explicit Noach reference.

entries.assessment: Read the full argument about apparent injustice, jealousy, unrecognized self-display, and the final recourse to prayer because hidden motives are not fully known even to their owner. Add Yisrael Kedoshim's developed example of Mordechai, distinguishing his own repair from the prosecution it could occasion against others.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after reading the whole paragraph: the Mordechai example explicitly separates a person's repair from harmful comparative prosecution and concludes with the same prayer against arousing another's envy.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach 14:2
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. It interprets perishing without judgment through premature calculation of redemption and the hidden good in a failed attempt, rather than the interpersonal consequences central here.

entries.assessment: Read the distinction between public pride and private self-satisfaction, Cain's disappointment, the forgotten strength of the inclination, and the need to recognize divine help even in mastery. Retain the Chanukah comparison's account of humility opening a person to Torah; the additional candidates do not warrant repeating the same image or verse.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Retained after full reading: the paragraph contrasts wisdom that recognizes only itself with humility through which Torah abides, then carefully distinguishes Torah's illuminating intention from the bare act.

Examined in full but not added: it repeats the empty-coin image and develops stable humility and awe; the existing comparison already supplies the relevant mechanism without another similar quotation.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 14
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not approved: its interpretation of sin crouching at the door concerns the limit of repentance during life, not Cain's mistaken self-assessment in this siman.

entries.assessment: Read the whole claim about a person's possessions sharing the soul's root, including animals, Noach's ark, family, and the explicit qualification that children continue the parents' acts. Add Mei HaShiloach's account of the creatures contributing to humanity and being elevated through human service; it explains participation in life rather than merely repeating an inheritance formula.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not added: it carefully distinguishes the collective identity of Israel through generations from an individual's parental liability, rather than explaining the root of possessions.
Examined in full but not added: the present mixture of opposites and different obligations at different levels do not supply the specific ownership-and-soul relation.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 6:1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full: the future disappearance of harmful separation fits the siman's future verse, but the more direct selected account explains the present relation of human and creature.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 3
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved: the complete short teaching expressly makes humanity a participant in all creatures' powers and explains how human service returns those powers to Hashem.

entries.assessment: Read the whole account of indirect consent to judgment, the examples of David, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Avraham, the discipline of speech, and the measure-for-measure consequence. The examined sources explain shared liability, association, and the ambiguity of Avraham's intercession, but do not sufficiently clarify the distinctive mechanism of an analogous verdict. No new conceptual note is approved in this finite pass.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but rejected: its logic of association and the proverb about a neighbor suffering do not explain indirect consent by judging an analogous case.

Examined in full but not approved: it explains why continued membership entails mutual responsibility and why Hoshea wished to separate sinners; that is not the same mechanism as unwittingly approving a decree.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 18:9
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not approved: it explains hidden generosity behind apparent constraint and Avraham's misunderstood intercession, not the exact relation between an analogous judgment and a decree.

entries.assessment: Read the full question of recognizing deviation when one’s path appears straight, and the answer locating its cause in the heart. Compared the two opposite kinds of apparent calm, but selected Mei HaShiloach’s fuller account of a cleared heart being filled by love rather than another desire. It explains the psychological mechanism of the straight path.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full but not selected: the complex account of Lot's daughters and wine concerns the redirection of the same instrument through intention, rather than diagnosing the feeling that one's own way is straight.
Examined in full: its contrast between wine exposing desire and wine occasioning joy in an upright heart is relevant, but Divrei Soferim states the needed psychological distinction more compactly.

Examined in full; not added. The distinction between quieted desire and satisfied desire is useful, but the selected Mei HaShiloach teaching more directly explains why examining the contents of the heart is essential.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 12:6
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. Unquestioned familiarity with Torah is distinguished from actual understanding, but the selected Divrei source more directly addresses desire and inward straightness.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after full reading, including the distinct concluding numerical allusion. The selected complete ethical unit explains why merely removing a desire leaves room for another, whereas love supplies the heart with a different content.

entries.assessment: Read the art of stopping speech at its proper boundary, the alternative explanation that Torah heals speech, and the distinction between a language and its independent wisdom. Add Sichat Malakhei HaSharet's precise account of ordinary speech becoming Torah through the speaker's chosen dedication; preserve its explicit denial that this status is automatic by birth.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after full reading: the paragraph explicitly interprets Torah coming out of the mouth almost of itself, including ordinary conversation, as the result of deliberate dedication rather than an inborn removal of choice.

Examined in full; not added. Voiced prayer awakening the inner voice corrects the impression of ownerless abundance, but it does not specifically explain the disciplined boundary between ordinary and Torah speech.

entries.assessment: Read the full mapping of Torah, changing souls, and the world's successive developments, including new Oral Torah and the concluding counsel proverb. Retain the existing account of differently composed souls. Add the Ishbitz account of Eliyahu and Ahab as an explicit example of a changing inner form and its outer counterpart.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full: the transition from prophecy to Oral Torah and the corresponding change from idolatry to the nations' wisdom is a strong historical illustration, but it need not be added alongside the selected, more compact two-school comparison.
Retained after reading the full paragraph: one Torah order is differently composed in each soul, and the same ordering of powers accounts for differences among worlds.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 11:1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after full reading: the storm-like form of Eliyahu's generation has an opposing storm in Ahab; changing divine governance changes the appropriate righteous form and its opposing counterpart.

entries.assessment: Read the complete account of acquisitions as degrees of one’s extended life, good and harmful creatures, the return to the divine source, Yaakov’s flocks, and respect for one’s livelihood. The selected Ishbitz explanation makes the difference between food as a garment and the divine utterance that gives life explicit; neither possession nor livelihood is an independent source.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. The destroyer and weapon verses concern Torah overcoming the inclination, rather than the relation of acquisitions to the life they sustain.

Examined in full, including the distinction between Rabbi and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and the final future-oriented qualification. Its account of wealth, desire, and holiness is relevant, but the selected Ishbitz source more directly explains the return of the acquired power to its source.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 46:4
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. Circumcision fixing recognition in the heart does not develop the particular ownership-and-life relation.

Approved after reading the whole teaching: the first omer unit explains food as a garment for the divine utterance and the return of its power to Hashem. Later units explicitly retain human service even after recognition becomes settled.

entries.assessment: Read the whole warning about a brief revelation followed by a return to desire, including the Flood generation, the seven days of Metushelach’s mourning, and the requirement of repentance even where atonement is opened from above. Add the Ishbitz distinction between freely given understanding and understanding acquired through labor, without treating a temporary gift as evidence of settled repair.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; rejected. The order of marriage and Torah study does not explain the durability of an unearned awakening.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:8
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. The initial divine gift and subsequent human work are relevant, but the selected source expressly explains why the first illumination can be forgotten.
Examined in full; not selected. Its account of shofar drawing life is less direct than the explicit distinction between gifted and acquired understanding.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 1:1
candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after full reading, including the later insistence that the child clarify his relationship through his own work. The selected complete contrast explains the transience of a gift received without effort.

entries.assessment: Read the full sequence of initial illumination, its loss, difficult recovery, compelled Sinai and willing Purim, and the greater Oral Torah of the Second Temple despite the absence of manifest Shekhinah. Retain the already placed Peri Tzadik explanation and add the Ishbitz definition of what remains after Torah study as a distinct account of permanence.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full: it develops the Second Temple, Oral Torah, and willing acceptance, but overlaps the already published Peri Tzadik comparison.

Retained after reading the complete paragraph. It explicitly values the Torah illumination acquired through adversity and quotes the greater Torah of the Second Temple alongside the absence of Shekhinah.
Approved after full reading. Its definition of the blessing after study supplies a separate criterion: Torah that remains firmly in the heart after the experience.

entries.assessment: Read the complete distinction between a face of wrath awakening fear and a face of favor reached through love, including the warning against diverting the awakening into frivolity. Add Rav Tzadok’s explicit ascent from self-concern through awe to love; do not treat all intense fear as the final aim.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; rejected. The warning about misuse of mystical language concerns a different mechanism from fear becoming love.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 8:2
candidatesReviewed.reason: Examined in full; not added. The moon illustrates renewal and familiarization, not the conversion of the face of wrath through awe.

candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 3
